question: How many real numbers satisfy the equation \(\sin(20\pi x) = \log_{20}(x)?\)
solution:
The sine range first confines all solutions to a finite interval. Its period then lets us count intersections one arch at a time.

Since \(-1\leq\sin(20\pi x)\leq1\), every solution satisfies
\[
\frac1{20}\leq x\leq20.
\]
Write \(L(x)=\log_{20}x\) and \(F(x)=\sin(20\pi x)-L(x)\). Both functions are continuous on this interval. Below \(1\), only negative sine arches can meet the negative logarithm; above \(1\), only positive arches can meet the positive logarithm.

We will justify the exact intersection counts without calculus. A graph is called concave when it lies above each chord, and convex when it lies below each chord. The logarithm is strictly concave: AM-GM gives
\[
L\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)\geq\frac{L(a)+L(b)}2,
\]
with strict inequality for \(a\ne b\). Repeated bisection and continuity give the corresponding inequality at every point of a chord. Similarly, the identity
\[
\frac{\sin\alpha+\sin\beta}{2}
=\sin\left(\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}\right)
\cos\left(\frac{\beta-\alpha}{2}\right)
\]
shows that a positive sine arch is strictly concave and a negative arch is strictly convex.

**Negative arches.** There are \(10\) of them, on
\[
\left[\frac{k}{10}+\frac1{20},\frac{k+1}{10}\right],
\qquad 0\leq k\leq9.
\]
At each left endpoint, \(F>0\). At each right endpoint, \(F>0\), except that \(F(1)=0\). At the midpoint of every arch, the sine equals \(-1\) while \(-1<L(x)<0\), so \(F<0\).

On each such interval, \(F\) is strictly convex because both the negative sine arch and \(-L\) are convex. A strictly convex function cannot have three zeros: the middle zero would have to lie strictly below the chord joining the outer two. The endpoint and midpoint signs therefore give exactly two roots per negative arch, counting \(x=1\) on the last arch. This contributes \(20\) roots.

**Positive arches.** There are \(190\) relevant arches, on
\[
\left[\frac{k}{10},\frac{k}{10}+\frac1{20}\right],
\qquad 10\leq k\leq199.
\]
At their endpoints, \(F<0\), except for \(F(1)=0\); at every peak, \(F=1-L(x)>0\). On each falling half, sine strictly decreases while \(L\) strictly increases, giving exactly one root.

It remains to prove that each rising half has at most one root. For a concave graph, secant slopes decrease as the intervals move right. Thus, for \(1\leq u<v\),
\[
\frac{L(v)-L(u)}{v-u}
\leq\frac{L(1)-L(1/2)}{1/2}
=2L(2)<1,
\]
since \(4<20\).

Suppose two roots \(u<v\) occur on one rising half. Every such half ends before \(399/20\). Comparing logarithm secant slopes on \([v,20]\) and \([20,40]\) gives
\[
\frac{1-L(v)}{20-v}\geq\frac{L(2)}{20}>\frac1{100},
\]
because \(2^5>20\) implies \(L(2)>1/5\). As \(20-v\geq1/20\), we obtain \(L(v)<1999/2000\).

Let \(\theta<\phi\) be the sine phases of \(u,v\), reduced to \([0,\pi/2]\). Since \(v\) is a root,
\[
\sin\phi=L(v)<\frac{1999}{2000},
\qquad
\cos\phi>\frac1{40}.
\]
Concavity of sine on \([0,\pi/2]\) gives the chord bound \(\sin t\geq2t/\pi\). The sine difference identity now yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sin\phi-\sin\theta
&=2\sin\left(\frac{\phi-\theta}{2}\right)
\cos\left(\frac{\phi+\theta}{2}\right)\\
&\geq\frac2\pi(\phi-\theta)\cos\phi\\
&>\frac2\pi\cdot20\pi(v-u)\cdot\frac1{40}
=v-u.
\end{aligned}
\]
But the logarithm comparison gave \(L(v)-L(u)<v-u\), contradicting that both points are roots. Hence every rising half has at most one root. Continuity supplies one, including the left-endpoint root \(x=1\) for the first positive arch.

The count is therefore:

| Relevant arches | Number of arches | Roots per arch | Roots counted |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Negative, below \(1\) | \(10\) | \(2\) | \(20\) |
| Positive, above \(1\) | \(190\) | \(2\) | \(380\) |

Only \(x=1\) appears in both rows. All other portions of the allowed interval have incompatible signs. Thus the number of distinct solutions is
\[
\boxed{20+380-1=399},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
